feedback: If a winner is announced before testing: ask 'how could we check?' and require pointing to what was observed before deciding.
If water amount or pour height varies between trays: model controlling variables \u2014 keep everything the same except the solution being tested, then re-run.
If the choice isn't tied to what happened: ask which tray's catch tray held the most soil and how that was seen or measured.
activities.intendedInsight: You judge which solution works best from evidence in a fair comparative test \u2014 keeping everything the same except the solution \u2014 rather than deciding by belief or by guessing from how a solution looks before testing.
learnerActions: First watch or recall how wind and water carry soil away from a slope, so the solutions have a clear purpose.

Set up three identical sloped trays of soil: one bare, one covered with living ground cover such as grass/moss (the cover shields the soil surface and roots, where present, bind it), one backed by a small retaining wall.
Pour the SAME amount of water from the SAME height over each tray, and catch the runoff/soil in a tray beneath each.

Measure or compare how much soil each slope lost (e.g. read a soil-loss catch tray or meter) and rank the three trays from least to most soil lost, using the bare tray as the no-protection comparison.
Name which solution worked best and point to the evidence you saw or measured to justify it.
State what you kept the same (water amount, pour height, slope) to make it a fair test.
Design and drop in your OWN barrier and test it the same way.
activities.title: Erosion-defence fair test: bare vs planted vs walled

feedback: If one solution is applied to every case without reasoning: contrast a wind case with a water case, and discuss why plant roots hold soil and why a wall can overtop.
If 'a wall always works' appears: point out barriers can fail, overtop, or shift, and ask what evidence would show that.
If cost/effort is ignored: prompt comparison of how much effort each solution takes against how much soil it saves.
activities.intendedInsight: There is rarely one perfect solution: the best choice depends on the situation (slope vs flat, wind vs water, cost/effort), and solutions have trade-offs; some solutions (like ground cover/plants) can help against more than one agent.
learnerActions: Compare a rainy slope scenario with a windy flat field scenario.

Decide which solution suits each situation: e.g. a windbreak (hedge/fence) to slow wind on the flat field, or a wall on a water slope \u2014 noting that plants/ground cover help reduce BOTH wind and water erosion because their roots bind the soil and the cover shields the surface.
Explain why one solution can beat another when the situation changes (water pooling/overtopping a wall, roots binding soil, wind vs water).
Consider cost/effort trade-offs for a site (e.g. 'the wall costs more \u2014 is it worth it here?') and justify your pick.
activities.title: Which solution for THIS situation? Surfacing trade-offs

feedback: If plants are seen as decoration or as causing erosion: show that roots bind and hold soil in place and ground cover shields the surface.
If the chart is misread: re-read the soil-lost column and compare the numbers directly.
Recognition and sorting support vocabulary but do not themselves show a learner can run and interpret a fair test \u2014 pair with the hands-on comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: Organising results into a comparison (solution \u2192 mechanism \u2192 how well it worked) lets you reason clearly about which solution wins and why.
learnerActions: Match each solution to how it helps (plants/roots \u2192 bind and hold soil, and the cover shields the surface; wall/terrace \u2192 block or hold back soil and water; windbreak \u2192 slow the wind).
Sort solutions by which eroding agent(s) they suit, remembering some solutions help against more than one.
Read a results chart (solution \u2192 how it helps \u2192 how much soil lost) and identify which slope lost the least soil.
Build a comparison chart from your own test results and use it to defend your claim.
activities.title: Reading and organising the comparison evidence
